report:
Your sister is correct. The evidence strongly supports that denosumab (Prolia) reduces the risk of vertebral fractures in osteoporosis.

**Key Evidence:**

The landmark study is the **FREEDOM trial** (Fracture Reduction Evaluation of Denosumab in Osteoporosis Every 6 Months), a 3-year randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 7,868 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 2009, it found that denosumab (60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months) reduced the relative risk of new vertebral fractures by **68%** compared to placebo. It also reduced hip fractures by 40% and nonvertebral fractures by 20% ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493); [AJMC summary](https://www.ajmc.com/view/study-summary-freedom)).

A 10-year extension study published in *The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology* (2017) confirmed that fracture incidence remained low over a decade of treatment, with rates similar to the initial three-year denosumab group and lower than projected placebo rates ([The Lancet](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landia/article/PIIS2213-8587(17)30138-9/fulltext)).

An independent review in *Drug Design, Development and Therapy* summarized that most evidence derives from the FREEDOM trials and concluded denosumab prevents both vertebral and non-vertebral fractures ([Dovepress](https://www.dovepress.com/a-review-on-the-role-of-denosumab-in-fracture-prevention-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT)). The American Academy of Family Physicians also noted denosumab is effective in reducing vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk ([AAFP](https://www.aafp.org/afp/2019/0501/od1)).

**Bottom line:** Multiple high-quality sources confirm denosumab significantly reduces vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal osteoporosis, with a 68% relative risk reduction in the pivotal trial.
